candidates.speaker: Frederick Copleston
candidates.proposition: Contingent beings and their totality require an external sufficient reason terminating in a being that cannot fail to exist.
candidates.attributionBasis: The passage is Copleston's announced, uninterrupted statement of his metaphysical argument from contingency.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is the principal constructive argument offered to establish God's existence through the contingency of experienced beings and the world.
candidates.contextSummary: After identifying contingency as his main line, Copleston moves from dependent beings through their aggregate to an external, self-explanatory necessary being.

candidates.speaker: Bertrand Russell
candidates.proposition: Necessity applies significantly only to analytic propositions, so a necessary being is admissible only if denying its existence is self-contradictory.
candidates.attributionBasis: Russell explicitly introduces this as his starting answer to Copleston's argument and develops it in one turn.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The objection challenges the intelligibility of the necessary being required by the contingency argument at its central inferential step.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Copleston's inference from contingent beings to a being that cannot fail to exist.

candidates.contextSummary: Russell begins his response by restricting necessity to analytic propositions and demanding that nonexistence of the proposed being entail a contradiction.

candidates.speaker: Frederick Copleston
candidates.proposition: Given an empirically discovered contingent being, the hypothetical proposition that a necessary being exists follows with necessity.
candidates.attributionBasis: Copleston states the conditional proposition, accepts Russell's terminology provisionally, and distinguishes its empirical premise.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move directly repairs the contested modal inference by separating the necessary conditional from the experiential discovery of contingency.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Russell's restriction of necessity to analytic propositions and denial of an intelligible necessary being.

candidates.contextSummary: Copleston treats the inference as a necessary conditional while acknowledging that the existence of its contingent premise must be learned through experience.

candidates.speaker: Bertrand Russell
candidates.proposition: The notions of necessary and contingent beings lack significance outside a rejected logical framework, because necessity applies to propositions rather than things.
candidates.attributionBasis: Russell directly states that he rejects both notions and explains his proposition-only use of the word necessary.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This denies that the modal categories supporting Copleston's entire metaphysical argument can meaningfully characterize existing beings at all.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Copleston's claim that an experienced contingent being entails the existence of a necessary being.

candidates.contextSummary: Russell responds that the disputed vocabulary has no usable interpretation for beings and confines meaningful necessity to analytic propositions.

candidates.speaker: Bertrand Russell
candidates.proposition: Treating a being's essence as involving existence revives the ontological argument, but existence is not a predicate and no named subject can exist analytically.
candidates.attributionBasis: Russell identifies the alleged ontological implication and then gives his logical account of meaningful existence claims.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move attacks the proposed necessary being by arguing that existence cannot be contained in an essence or asserted analytically of a named subject.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Copleston's definition of a necessary being as one that must exist and cannot fail to exist.

candidates.contextSummary: Russell recasts Copleston's necessary being as an ontological argument and objects that meaningful existence attaches to descriptions, not as a predicate of named subjects.

candidates.speaker: Frederick Copleston
candidates.proposition: God's existence is inferred from experience rather than from an a priori grasp of divine essence, after which essence and existence must be identified.
candidates.attributionBasis: Copleston expressly distinguishes his experiential inference from an argument based solely on an intuition of God's essence.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This preserves the contingency argument against the ontological-argument objection while explaining why the inferred terminus cannot require a further reason.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Russell's objection that a necessary being illegitimately makes existence analytic or part of a subject's essence.

candidates.contextSummary: Copleston says experience first establishes the being, while the identity of divine essence and existence follows because otherwise a reason beyond God would be required.

candidates.speaker: Bertrand Russell
candidates.proposition: Although particular things may have causes, there is no reason to suppose that their totality has any cause whatsoever.
candidates.attributionBasis: Russell grants causal explanation for a particular object and immediately rejects extending that concept to the totality.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The objection targets the aggregation step that moves from explanations of individual contingent things to an explanation of the world as a whole.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Copleston's demand to extend causal or sufficient-reason inquiry from particular objects to their totality.

candidates.contextSummary: Russell accepts ordinary causal inquiry within the world but denies that observation of particular causes supplies any basis for a cause of the whole.

candidates.speaker: Frederick Copleston
candidates.proposition: Mystical experience is best explained by an objective transcendent cause because its basic character cannot be explained adequately as purely subjective.
candidates.attributionBasis: Copleston announces the religious-experience topic, defines the relevant experience, and states his explanatory inference.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is the principal constructive case concerning whether religious experience supplies grounds for affirming an objective divine reality.
candidates.contextSummary: Copleston disclaims strict proof, describes a loving awareness of a transcendent and nonconceptual object, and argues that an objective cause best explains it.

candidates.speaker: Bertrand Russell
candidates.proposition: Private mystical reports do not establish God because equally convinced reports concern demons or Satan, which Copleston would not accept on the same basis.
candidates.attributionBasis: Russell states his agnostic conclusion and compares mystical testimony with similarly confident reports of rejected supernatural beings.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The parity objection directly contests the evidential force of religious experience by showing that the proposed method supports incompatible supernatural conclusions.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Copleston's claim that mystical experience is best explained by an objectively existing transcendent divine cause.

candidates.contextSummary: Russell argues that recorded mystical conviction must be treated like other testimony and cannot favor God when phenomenologically similar experiences support Satan or demons.

candidates.speaker: Bertrand Russell
candidates.proposition: A profound and wholesome transformation caused by an experience is not evidence that the experience involved any reality outside the subject.
candidates.attributionBasis: Russell appeals to his own transformative experiences and explicitly denies that their effects evidence an external object.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move rebuts the proposed use of morally beneficial consequences as corroboration for the objective reference or truth of mystical experience.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Copleston's appeal to the transformed and benevolent lives of mystics as support for their experiential claims.

candidates.contextSummary: Russell observes that experiences can deeply improve a person's character without involving anything external and denies that wholesome effects verify an external interpretation.
